#step-by-step recipe with which you solved the (protein weight calculator) task in R
The first stage involves establishing a computational framework by defining an R function. This function utilizes a default input parameter, which serves as a placeholder for any protein sequence provided for analysis. Within this environment, a named vector is constructed to function as a digital dictionary. Each entry in this dictionary pairs a specific one-letter amino acid code, such as "A" for Alanine, with its corresponding molecular weight in Daltons. This structure allows the system to retrieve specific numerical values based on character keys.
The second stage focuses on preparing the raw input for data mapping. To prevent errors caused by inconsistent capitalization, the input string is processed through the toupper () function, standardizing all characters to uppercase. Following this, the strsplit () function is employed to decompose the continuous string of text into a list of individual characters. This conversion is essential because it allows the software to evaluate each "building block" of the protein sequence independently.
The third stage involves the cross-referencing of characters against the weight dictionary. During this lookup process, characters that do not correspond to recognized amino acids, such as the letter "B," return a value of NA (Not Available). To maintain the integrity of the calculation, a logical safety net is applied to identify these missing values and replace them with a numerical value of 0. This step ensures that the presence of non-protein characters does not cause the mathematical operation to fail, ensuring only valid biological data contributes to the total.
The final stage completes the procedure through arithmetic summation and unit conversion. The sum () function is used to aggregate the individual weights of all recognized characters into a total molecular mass. In scientific practice, these values are typically expressed in Kilodaltons (kDa) rather than Daltons (Da) to make large numbers more manageable.
